title: Scaling Writes
summary: Protect the write path with batching, partitioning, queues, and honest limits.
keyPoints: Write throughput is limited by fsync, locks, indexes, and replication, not only CPU.
Group commit and batching trade a small latency increase for much higher throughput.
A durable queue absorbs bursts but cannot create capacity; bound it and shed load when consumers fall behind.
Partition writes on a high-cardinality key, and give hot keys their own treatment.
LSM-trees favor write-heavy workloads by appending, then pay for compaction later.
Async writes need status tracking, idempotency, and a read-your-writes plan.

complexity.note: A size or time limit caps added latency.
Consumer lag is the real risk.
A hot shard can still overload one node.

commonMistakes: Adding a queue in front of a saturated database and calling it scaling.
Using a sequential ID as a partition key and sending every insert to one shard.
Acknowledging an async write before it is durable or discoverable.
Watching queue length while ignoring the age of the oldest item.
interviewNotes: Separate read scaling from write scaling; the fixes are different.
Name the write bottleneck: fsync, lock contention, index maintenance, replication, or a hot partition.
If you batch, state the batch size, the time window, and the tail-latency cost.
Say how the queue is bounded and what happens when it fills.
For async writes, show the status endpoint and the read-your-writes strategy.

checkYourself.question: Why does group commit increase write throughput?
checkYourself.answer: Several writes share one disk flush, so the expensive durability step is amortized across the batch. The trade-off is a short wait while the batch fills.

checkYourself.question: What does a queue in front of a database actually solve?
checkYourself.answer: It absorbs bursts and decouples producers from consumers. It does not increase the database's sustained write capacity, so a backlog still grows when producers are faster.

checkYourself.question: Why can a hot key defeat sharding?
checkYourself.answer: Sharding distributes keys, not individual key traffic. One key with a large share of writes still maps to one shard, which becomes the bottleneck.
